title: Dogs-R-Us pet store: journalizing a week of cash receipts and payments, reconciling cash and interpreting results
participant_role: Accounting manager for Dogs-R-Us, a retail store for dog food and toys
judge_role: Owner of Dogs-R-Us who wants the week's cash recorded and insight into the cash position
scenario:
You are to assume the role of the accounting manager for DOGS-R-US, a retail store dedicated to dog food and toys. The owner of DOGS-R-US (judge) has asked you to record both cash receipts and payments for the most recent week. In addition, the owner (judge) would like for you to provide some insight as to the company's cash position at the end of the week.

The following is the most recent week's cash receipts and payments:

1. Customer purchases of premium pet food totaling $183.00.
2. Multiple customers purchased various pet toys throughout the week, totaling cash receipts of $420.00.
3. A cash payment of $100.00 was made for a local newspaper ad promoting a weekend sale.
4. Customers purchased collars and leashes for $75.00.
5. The store spent $150.00 in cash to purchase new display racks for showcasing pet toys and accessories.
6. A customer paid $25.00 in cash to join the membership loyalty program for discounts and benefits.
7. The store paid $200.00 in cash to a local supplier for a quick restock of popular pet food brands.
8. A cash payment of $60.00 was made for cleaning supplies and miscellaneous store maintenance items.

In a meeting with the owner (judge) you must:
- Provide journal entries to record cash receipts and payments.
- Reconcile cash to obtain a balance for the week.
- Summarize the weekly results and provide any insights regarding the cash transactions.

You will present the information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's (judge's) office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

solution.overview: A strong answer journalizes each of the eight items (debit Cash for the four receipts against sales revenue accounts; credit Cash for the four payments against advertising expense, supplies expense, inventory and repair and maintenance), reconciles cash as $703 of receipts less $510 of payments for a net cash increase of $193, and then interprets the week: cash flow was positive, the display racks are a one-time cost, toys outsold food, and food inventory restocking roughly matched food sales, which raises stock-level and margin questions.

answer: 1. Debit Cash $183, credit Sales Revenue (food) $183
2. Debit Cash $420, credit Sales Revenue (toys) $420
4. Debit Cash $75, credit Sales Revenue (supplies) $75
6. Debit Cash $25, credit Sales Revenue (loyalty program) $25
Cost of goods sold and inventory reductions for the sales are not recorded here because they have no cash impact
3. Debit Advertising Expense $100, credit Cash $100
5. Debit Supplies Expense $150, credit Cash $150 (display racks; could also be treated as store equipment)
7. Debit Inventory (food) $200, credit Cash $200
8. Debit Repair and Maintenance Expense $60, credit Cash $60
Total cash receipts: $183 + $420 + $75 + $25 = $703
Total cash payments: $100 + $150 + $200 + $60 = $510
Net cash for the week: $703 - $510 = $193 increase
Compare the $193 to the actual change in the cash register and bank account to confirm nothing is missing
Cash receipts exceeded cash payments, which is positive for the company
The $150 for display racks is a one-time cost, so net cash should be higher in future weeks; advertising may also be infrequent
The $200 food restock was about the same as the $183 of food sales; without gross margin data it is hard to judge, and the store may run short of food choices in coming weeks
No pet toy inventory was purchased even though toys were the top seller ($420), so check toy stock levels
Toys generated more cash than food; this may be a one-off or a real customer preference, so consider a marketing campaign aimed at dog food sales

judge_question_answers.question: If the store made a donation to the local animal shelter, how would that be journaled?
answer: A cash donation: debit Charitable Contributions (Donation) Expense, credit Cash for the amount given
If the store donated pet food or toys from stock: debit Donation Expense, credit Inventory at the cost of the items
It is a cash payment (or inventory reduction), not a sale, so it lowers net cash and net income; keep the receipt for tax purposes

judge_question_answers.question: If a customer returns a product, how do we include that in the weekly results?
answer: Record a cash refund: debit Sales Returns and Allowances (a contra-revenue account), credit Cash
The refund counts as a cash payment in the weekly reconciliation, reducing net cash and net sales
Put the returned item back into Inventory if it can be resold (debit Inventory, credit Cost of Goods Sold), otherwise write it off

key_concepts.definition: Cash coming into the business, mainly from cash sales and customer payments; recorded with a debit to Cash.
Cash going out for expenses, inventory or assets; recorded with a credit to Cash.
Comparing recorded receipts and payments to the actual cash on hand or in the bank: Beginning cash + receipts - payments = ending cash.
Total cash receipts minus total cash payments; here $703 - $510 = $193.
Income earned from selling goods or services; credited when a sale is made.
Goods bought to resell (pet food) are recorded as Inventory, an asset; items used up in running the store (ads, cleaning supplies) are expenses.
The cost of inventory sold to customers; recorded when goods are sold but has no cash effect, so it is left out of a cash-only analysis.
Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold; shows how much each sale contributes before operating expenses.
One-time costs such as display racks will not repeat weekly, so future net cash should be higher; recurring costs like restocking happen every period.
A contra-revenue account used when customers return goods or receive refunds; it reduces net sales.
The account used when a business donates cash or goods; it reduces net income and may be tax deductible.
Owners use records like the weekly cash summary to see whether cash is growing, which products sell, what to restock and where to spend on marketing.
